pages.name: Gods = Tulpas = Human Ideas Brought To Life Via Belief

text.content:
🟣 GODHOOD AS COMMUNITY SERVICE (BBTTCC Canon)

“There are no gods. There are only positions.”

The BBTTCC cosmos is alive, reactive, and extremely bureaucratic, and here is the natural metaphysical consequence:

🟩 1. “Gods” are not divine beings — they are long-lived, well-funded thoughtforms.

Not metaphorically.
Literally:

They are artificially sustained Tulpas created by collective attention & metaphysical investment.

When enough people believe in a vibe — love, war, accounting, rain, awkward silence, tacos — that vibe becomes:

• a template
• a pattern
• a self-hosting metaphysical process
• and eventually a semi-autonomous entity

They start as memetic weather but can crystallize into Civic Deities.

You don’t pray to them because they’re superior.
You pray to them because:

“Somebody has to hold the Concept of Rain so it doesn’t leak.”

Wizards, at this point, roll their eyes so hard they sprain a ley-line.

🟩 2. The Ancient Problem: Raw Magic Tries to Leave Through the Head.

Before the Tulpal Model of Divinity was perfected, personal magic was basically:

✨ “Brain Pressure + Poor Life Choices = Spontaneous Metaphysical Ejection” ✨

Early wizards:

  • Overchanneled

  • Exploded, gently or otherwise

  • Produced local anomalies

  • Became fond of claiming they were gods, even though they were really just concussed

So the civilization developed a workaround:

➤ You funnel your magic through a conceptual being.

➤ You let the Tulpa handle the metaphysical overflow.

➤ Your brain stays inside your skull.

Problem solved!
Mostly!

(Except for the wizard guild, who publicly denounced it while adopting it privately.)

🟩 3. Civilization eventually industrialized Tulpamancy.

Once metaphysics was understood, the ancient city-states realized:

“Wait… if deities are just optimized thoughtforms,
and we understand cognition,
then we can manufacture gods.”

And so they did.
Not as tyrants.
Not as omniscient beings.

But as civic infrastructure.

Like:

  • “Goddess of Transit Efficiency”

  • “Lord Archivist of Weather Records”

  • “Spirit of Waste Management”

  • “Minor Angel of Don’t Touch That”

  • “The Saint of People Who Really Tried”

They were utility processes delegated to:

• maintain conceptual stability
• handle metaphysical ticket queues
• buffer emotional resonance
• reduce magic leakage
• store surplus prayer-energy
• keep wizards from sucking raw ley-field directly out of the ground (“DO NOT DRINK THAT”)

Effectively:

Gods were a public utility grid.

And society treated them with that exact level of respect:

→ Reverent enough to maintain
→ Annoyed enough to complain about outages

🟩 4. Becoming a God Was Literally Jury Duty.

Every citizen was, technically, eligible.

The metaphysical process went like:

  1. A deity’s coherence decays (entropy, story-death, negligence, wizard involvement).

  2. The community must elect—or draft—a new host.

  3. Host provides biological anchoring.

  4. Tulpa overlays into their cognition but does NOT override personality.

  5. They hold the concept until:

  • the job is done

  • their term ends

  • they burn out

  • they get promoted (?)

  • they literally ascend into a conceptual storage cloud

  • or they file an early resignation (“please let me go home now”)

Coraliindra is EXACTLY this:
A divinity-as-professional, performing Godhood as Community Service because she was chosen, not because she was born superior.

She’s the poster child for the old metaphysical motto:

“Godhood isn’t a privilege.
It’s a shift.”
